paragraphs.heading: Current, voltage and resistance
paragraphs.text: Ohm's law links three quantities for a conductor: the current I flowing through it, the voltage V measured across it, and its resistance R. The conductance, written G, is simply 1/R. The core of the law is that R stays constant whatever the current. If the resistance changes with the current, the relation can no longer be called Ohm's law, though it can still be used to define static, or DC, resistance.

paragraphs.heading: Where it holds
paragraphs.text: Ohm's law is an empirical relation. It describes how the great majority of conducting materials carry current, and it stays accurate over many orders of magnitude of current. Some materials break it, and these are called non-ohmic. The law can also be written for a single location inside a material, linking the current density J there to the electric field E through σ, the conductivity, which is the inverse of the resistivity ρ. Gustav Kirchhoff gave the law this form.

paragraphs.heading: Cavendish's shocks
paragraphs.text: Before Georg Ohm's work, in January 1781, Henry Cavendish ran experiments with Leyden jars and with glass tubes of salt solution of different widths and lengths. He judged the current by how strong a shock he felt when he closed the circuit with his own body. He wrote that current varied directly with voltage. He did not share the result with other scientists, and it stayed unknown until James Clerk Maxwell published it in 1879.

paragraphs.heading: Ohm's experiments
paragraphs.text: Georg Ohm, a German physicist, studied resistance during 1825 and 1826, then in 1827 brought out his findings in a book titled Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet. He started with voltaic piles as his source but later switched to a thermocouple, which gave a steadier voltage. He measured current with a galvanometer and completed the circuit with test wires of different lengths, diameters and materials. His readings fit the equation x = a/(b + ℓ), in which the galvanometer reading is x and the test wire's length is ℓ. From this he arrived at his law of proportionality.

paragraphs.heading: A hostile welcome
paragraphs.text: Today the law seems almost obvious, but it did not when Ohm first published. Critics met his work with hostility and called it a "web of naked fancies". The leading scientific view in Germany then held that nature is so orderly that its truths can be found by reasoning alone, with no need for experiments. His work was not widely accepted until the 1840s, and by the 1850s the law was widely known and regarded as proved.

paragraphs.heading: Why it works
paragraphs.text: In 1900 Paul Drude proposed the Drude model, the first classical model of electrical conduction, and it finally explained the law. It pictures a solid conductor as a fixed lattice of atoms with conduction electrons moving about at random among them. A voltage creates an electric field that speeds the electrons along, and their overall drift is the current. The electrons keep colliding with atoms, which scatters them and turns their energy of motion into heat. On average, the drift speed, and with it the current, comes out proportional to the field, and so to the voltage, over a wide range of voltages.

paragraphs.heading: The quantum picture
paragraphs.text: Quantum mechanics, developed in the 1920s, changed this picture somewhat. Modern theories can still show that the average drift speed of electrons is proportional to the electric field, which gives Ohm's law. Felix Bloch showed that electrons travel through a crystal lattice as waves. They scatter mainly off impurity atoms and defects, not off the lattice atoms as the Drude model supposed.
